messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 72-year-old African American Coast Guard veteran, has been grappling with the aftermath of a toxic chemical exposure incident that occurred during his service. The event left him feeling deeply vulnerable and ever on guard against potential threats. John’s marriage remains stable but strained due to his increasing isolation. The trauma began when he was stationed near an industrial plant where a major leak of toxic chemicals had occurred. As he approached the site, the silence was overwhelming; no sounds of machinery or workers—just eerie quiet. Suddenly, a strong wind carried a cloud of chemicals towards him, and he could feel it burning his skin and eyes as he tried to escape. The fear and helplessness he experienced during that moment have lingered ever since. John has come to believe that the world is an inherently dangerous place, a conviction that exacerbates his feelings of vulnerability. This belief makes even mundane moments, like the silence in his home when his wife is at work, feel threatening. “Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen,” he says, describing how the stillness triggers intense anxiety and physical reactions such as racing heartbeats and sweating. His memories of that day replay in vivid detail—like a film loop—whenever he hears or sees anything that reminds him of that incident. When these memories return, they overwhelm him with intense emotions, making it difficult to function. The photographic recall makes the experience feel immediate and real, as if he is reliving it every time. John has come to believe that he can’t deal with even the slightest upset, which only reinforces his sense of danger. His thoughts are constantly drawn back to the event, and he fears that if he allows himself to think about it, he will not be able to handle the intensity of the emotions that arise. This thought avoidance leads him to avoid places and situations where such memories might surface. The cycle begins with John feeling on guard even inside his own home—a space where he should feel safe but doesn’t. The memory replay reinforces this sense of danger; every time he remembers the event, the physical reactions are so strong that they trigger more fear. His low coping ability means that these reactions are overwhelming and difficult to manage. John's world has become a series of avoidances. He has stopped attending social gatherings and even avoids going out for walks in his neighborhood, as the silence can quickly escalate into feelings of impending danger. This isolation has strained his relationship with his wife, who feels frustrated by his increasing withdrawal. His fear that the world is inherently dangerous has led him to feel constantly on edge. The memory of the chemical exposure plays over and over, each time reinforcing his belief that he cannot cope with any form of threat or stress. This self-reinforcing loop has left John feeling trapped in a cycle of anxiety and avoidance, making it difficult for him to engage fully in daily life. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that his wife could not continue living like this—both their worlds had shrunk too much. He is most afraid of being unable to protect himself or those he loves from danger but hopes that with support, he can regain a sense of safety and control over his life.
